Bayesian estimation of the Benter ranking model

Source: R/gibbsBenter.R
gibbsBenter.Rd

Fits the Benter (1994) model for ranking data by Gibbs sampling. The Benter model generalizes the Plackett-Luce model by introducing stage-specific dampening exponents \(\alpha_r \in (0, 1]\) that down-weight the information in later ranking stages: $$p(\pi_i \mid \lambda, \alpha) = \prod_{r=1}^{J-1} \frac{\lambda_{w_{ir}}^{\alpha_r}}{\sum_{j \in R_{ir}} \lambda_j^{\alpha_r}},$$ where \(\lambda_j > 0\) are item worths, \(w_{ir}\) is the item placed \(r\)th by voter \(i\), and \(R_{ir}\) is the set of items still at risk at stage \(r\). Inference uses a positive-stable frailty data augmentation that restores conjugacy, so the worths are drawn exactly from Gamma full conditionals while each \(\alpha_r\) is updated by Metropolis-Hastings on its collapsed conditional.

Usage

gibbsBenter(
  pi,
  J,
  a,
  b,
  c,
  d,
  alpha_min = 0,
  iters = 1000,
  mh_iters = 5,
  burnin = 0.5,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

pi

A ranking data set: an integer matrix (or data frame, or a single vector interpreted as one ranking) with one ranking per row. Entry pi[i, r] is the item placed rth by voter i; ranked entries are left-aligned and any unranked tail positions are NA. All non-missing entries must be integers in 1:J with no repeats within a row.

J

Integer (>= 3). The total number of items being ranked.

a, b

Shape and rate of the Gamma(a, b) prior on the item worths \(\lambda_j\). On the identified (sum-to-one) scale, a alone controls the induced symmetric Dirichlet prior on the normalized worths; b only sets the (marginalized-out) overall scale.

c, d

Shape parameters of the Beta(c, d) prior on each dampening exponent \(\alpha_r\), r=2,...,J-1. (alpha_1 is fixed at 1 for identifiability.)

alpha_min

Lower floor for the Metropolis-Hastings proposals of \(\alpha_r\). Proposals at or below alpha_min are rejected. A small positive value (e.g. 0.05) keeps alpha_r inside the range where the tilted-stable sampler is numerically stable; the default 0 imposes no floor beyond the open boundary.

iters

Number of Gibbs iterations (including burn-in).

mh_iters

Number of Metropolis-Hastings sub-steps per \(\alpha_r\) per sweep.

burnin

Fraction of iters discarded as burn-in. The adaptive tuning of the proposal scales is active during burn-in and frozen afterwards.

verbose

Logical. If TRUE, show a text progress bar.

Value

A list with components:

lambda

A (iters - burn) x J matrix of posterior draws of the item worths, normalized to sum to one in each row.

alpha

A (iters - burn) x (J-1) matrix of posterior draws of the dampening exponents. Column 1 is fixed at 1; for partial data, columns beyond the deepest observed rank are NA.

parameters

A list recording the prior and sampler settings and the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rates.

time_secs

Wall-clock run time in seconds.

Details

gibbsBenter() is the user-facing entry point. It validates and standardizes pi, then dispatches to the appropriate internal sampler for complete or partial rankings. A length-(J-1) ranking pins down its final item and is completed automatically (this is deduction, not imputation); a row is treated as genuinely partial only if it leaves two or more items unplaced.

For partial rankings, only the dampening parameters up to the deepest observed rank are identifiable, so alpha_r for stages beyond the longest observed ranking are neither updated nor returned (reported as NA). The item worths \(\lambda\) for all J items are always estimated.

References

Benter, W. (1994). Computer-based horse race handicapping and wagering systems: A report. In Efficiency of Racetrack Betting Markets.

See also

rBenter() to simulate rankings from the model.

Examples

set.seed(1)
lambda <- c(5, 3, 2, 1.5, 1)
lambda <- lambda / sum(lambda)
alpha  <- c(1, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7)
pi <- rBenter(200, lambda, alpha)

# \donttest{
fit <- gibbsBenter(pi, J = 5, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1, d = 1,
                   iters = 400, burnin = 0.5)
colMeans(fit$lambda)   # posterior mean worths (vs. truth `lambda`)
#> [1] 0.41990139 0.20843699 0.18133789 0.10639968 0.08392406
colMeans(fit$alpha)    # posterior mean dampening (vs. truth `alpha`)
#> [1] 1.0000000 0.8617744 0.7392397 0.6400031
# }
